title: Generic Class in Java - GeeksforGeeks
content:
A generic class in Java is a class that uses type parameters to work with different data types while maintaining compile-time type safety. The actual type is specified when an object of the generic class is created.

  • The same class can work with types such as Integer, String, or custom classes.
  • Generic type parameters use reference types and cannot directly use primitive types such as int or double.
Java 
class Box<T> {
    private T data;

    public void setData(T data) { this.data = data; }

    public T getData() { return data; }
}

public class Geeks {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {

        Box<Integer> intBox = new Box<>();
        intBox.setData(10);

        Box<String> stringBox = new Box<>();
        stringBox.setData("GeeksforGeeks");

        System.out.println(intBox.getData());
        System.out.println(stringBox.getData());
    }
}

Output
10
GeeksforGeeks

Explanation:

  • Box<T> declares T as a type parameter.
  • Box<Integer> creates a Box that works with Integer values.
  • Box<String> creates another Box that works with String values.
  • The compiler checks that only values compatible with the specified type are used.

Syntax

The general syntax of a generic class is:

class ClassName<T> {
T variable;

T methodName() {
return variable;
}
}

Here:

  • T represents a type parameter.
  • The type parameter is declared after the class name using < >.
  • T can be used for fields, method parameters, and return types within the class.

Generic Class with Single Type Parameter

A generic class can define a single type parameter, such as T, which acts as a placeholder for an actual data type. The type is specified when an object of the generic class is created, allowing the same class to work with different types.

Syntax:

class ClassName<T> {
T data;
}

Java 
class Box<T> {
    private T data;

    public void setData(T data) { this.data = data; }

    public T getData() { return data; }
}

public class Geeks {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        Box<Integer> intBox = new Box<>();
        Box<String> stringBox = new Box<>();

        intBox.setData(100);
        stringBox.setData("Java");

        System.out.println(intBox.getData());
        System.out.println(stringBox.getData());
    }
}

Output
100
Java

Explanation: The Box<T> class uses T as a type parameter. When Box<Integer> is created, T represents Integer, while in Box<String>, T represents String, allowing the same class to store different types safely.

Generic Class with Multiple Type Parameters

A generic class can also define multiple type parameters when it needs to work with more than one type. The type parameters are declared inside angle brackets and separated by commas, such as <K, V>.

Syntax:

class ClassName<T, U> {
T first;
U second;
}

Java 
class Pair<K, V> {
    private K key;
    private V value;

    public Pair(K key, V value)
    {
        this.key = key;
        this.value = value;
    }

    public K getKey() { return key; }

    public V getValue() { return value; }
}

public class Geeks {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        Pair<Integer, String> pair = new Pair<>(101, "Java");

        System.out.println("Key: " + pair.getKey());
        System.out.println("Value: " + pair.getValue());
    }
}

Output
Key: 101
Value: Java

Explanation: The Pair<K, V> class declares two type parameters. In Pair<Integer, String>, K represents Integer and V represents String, allowing the object to store values of two different types.

Generic Classes with Custom Types

Generic classes are not limited to built-in classes such as Integer and String. A custom class can also be used as a type argument.

Java 
class Student {
    String name;

    Student(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

class Box<T> {
    private T data;

    public void setData(T data) { this.data = data; }

    public T getData() { return data; }
}

public class Geeks {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        Box<Student> studentBox = new Box<>();

        studentBox.setData(new Student("Akshat"));

        Student student = studentBox.getData();
        System.out.println(student.name);
    }
}

Output
Akshat

Explanation: Box<Student> specifies Student as the type argument. Therefore, the Box object stores and returns Student objects while maintaining compile-time type checking.

Generic Classes and Primitive Types

Java generics work with reference types, so primitive types such as int, double, and char cannot be directly used as generic type arguments.

For example, this is invalid:

Box<int> box = new Box<>(); // Invalid

Instead, use the corresponding wrapper class:

Box<Integer> box = new Box<>(); // Valid

Some common primitive and wrapper combinations are:

Primitive TypeWrapper Class
intInteger
doubleDouble
charCharacter
booleanBoolean
longLong

Bounded Type Parameters in Generic Classes

Sometimes, a generic class should accept only a particular category of types. Bounded type parameters allow us to restrict the types that can be used.

Syntax:

class ClassName<T extends Type> {
// Class body
}

Java 
class NumberBox<T extends Number> {
    private T number;

    NumberBox(T number) { this.number = number; }

    public T getNumber() { return number; }
}

public class Geeks {
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        NumberBox<Integer> obj1 = new NumberBox<>(100);
        NumberBox<Double> obj2 = new NumberBox<>(25.5);

        System.out.println(obj1.getNumber());
        System.out.println(obj2.getNumber());
    }
}
Try It Yourself

Output
100
25.5

Explanation: T extends Number restricts the type parameter to Number or its subclasses. Therefore, types such as Integer and Double are allowed, while String is not.
